screens.title: Lifecycle Environments and Host Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we build a reliable content delivery pipeline using Lifecycle Environments and host management in Red Hat Satellite. You will learn what a lifecycle environment is, how to create an environment path that models Development, QA, and Production, and why promoting versioned Content Views through those stages reduces risk. We will cover host registration using activation keys so that a client is automatically assigned an organization, a Content View, and the correct environment. You will also see how subscription status and Candlepin entitlements control whether a host can receive updates. Finally, we'll walk through applying errata and package updates from Satellite to managed hosts. For example, a security patch synchronized to Satellite must be published in a new Content View version and promoted through lower stages before Production sees it. That practice ensures changes are tested and predictable. As you proceed, keep an eye out for two common mistakes: forgetting to publish new Content View versions after synchronization, and misconfigured activation keys that assign hosts to the wrong environment. By the end you'll understand the lifecycle flow, practical host registration, and how to keep systems compliant and patched without disrupting production.

screens.title: What is a Lifecycle Environment?
screens.narratorSegment: A Lifecycle Environment is an explicit stage that represents where a Content View version is allowed to be used. Think of it as a labeled container — Development, QA, Staging, Production — that controls the repositories and package snapshots visible to enrolled hosts. Defining environments establishes a promotion path: you decide that content moves from Library to Development, then QA, and finally Production, and Satellite enforces that flow. A concrete example: after synchronizing security errata into Satellite, you publish a new Content View version. That version initially exists in the Library. You must publish it and then promote it to Development so testers can validate the updates. Only after validation do you promote it onward. A common misconception is believing synchronization alone makes updates available to production. It does not. Content View versions are immutable snapshots; only publishing a new version and promoting it makes the new content visible to a target environment. Why this matters in practice: it prevents accidental rollout of untested packages to production. As a closing checkpoint, ask yourself: what would happen if you promoted directly to Production without a Development stage?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Lifecycle Environment is a named stage that gates which Content View versions are accessible to hosts.

content.html:
Core Concept › Lifecycle Environment
What it means
An explicit stage such as Development or Production that controls which Content View versions are available to hosts.
  • Environments form a parent-child promotion path.
  • Content View versions must be published and then promoted.
  • Hosts only see content from their assigned environment.
Key Takeaway

Promotions, not syncs, control when hosts get updated content.

Analogy & example
Analogy: Think of Library as the raw build area and each Lifecycle Environment as a QA gate. Example: publish CV 1.1, promote to Development, test, then promote to Production.
Common misconception
Syncing repos does not make packages visible to Production. You must publish a new Content View version and promote it to the target environment.

screens.title: Creating a Lifecycle Environment Path
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a lifecycle environment path is a simple but crucial process. In Satellite you go to Content → Lifecycle Environments and add named environments. Each environment you add can specify a parent, which creates the promotion path. A typical setup is Library as the root, Development with parent Library, and Production with parent Development. The practical effect is that when you promote a Content View version you choose a target environment and Satellite enforces where that copy appears. Concrete example: create Development with parent Library, then create Production with parent Development. Now publish CV version 2.0. Promote 2.0 to Development and test. Only after testing do you promote 2.0 to Production. A common error is reversing parent relationships or creating isolated environments that break the flow. Another pitfall is treating Library as a deployable environment — it is a repository of synchronized content, not an environment for production hosts. Verify your path by reviewing the environment tree and confirming that promotion actions show the expected next step. How would you validate that a new environment path allows promotion from Dev to Prod without bypassing QA?

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Define parent-child relationships so Content View versions flow through a controlled promotion path.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create environment path
Step-by-step
  1. Open Content → Lifecycle Environments in Satellite UI.
  2. Create Development with parent Library.
  3. Create Production with parent Development.
  4. Publish and promote Content View versions along this path.
Verification: the environment tree shows Library → Development → Production and promotion actions list the next environment.
Common mistakes & checks
  • Don't set the wrong parent order; promotions will not reach intended targets.
  • Don't treat Library as a production environment; it's the synchronization container.
  • Check promotion history to ensure versions traveled the expected path.
Try this
Create a two-stage path: Dev → Prod, publish a small Content View change, and promote through Dev to verify history and availability.

screens.title: Promoting a Content View via CLI
screens.narratorSegment: The hammer CLI provides a reproducible way to list Content View versions and promote a specific version into a lifecycle environment. The first useful command is listing versions for a given Content View so you can identify the version string to promote. Next, use the promote command, specifying the target lifecycle environment and organization. A concrete example from the chapter shows promoting version 1.0 of a Content View called 'Base RHEL 8 & Custom Apps' to Development. Running these commands in automation ensures repeatability and records the action in Satellite's task history. A common misconception is thinking promotion mutates a version — promotions copy immutable versions into the target environment rather than modifying the original. If you automate promotions, include checks that the target environment exists and that the version was published. As a closing thought, decide whether CLI promotion or UI promotion fits your workflow better: CLI is scriptable and auditable, UI is visual and helpful for ad-hoc checks. Which method would you choose for a large-scale automated pipeline? Promoting a Content View via CLI means use hammer to identify and promote immutable content view versions into lifecycle environments for repeatable change control.. In practical terms, use hammer to list versions and promote reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CLI promotion
keyIdea.text: Use hammer to identify and promote immutable Content View versions into lifecycle environments for repeatable change control.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › hammer content-view promotion
List versions
# Find the latest version of your Content View
hammer content-view version list --content-view "Base RHEL 8 & Custom Apps" --organization "MyOrg"
Promote a version
# Promote version 1.0 to Development
hammer content-view version promote --content-view "Base RHEL 8 & Custom Apps" \
                                   --version "1.0" \
                                   --to-lifecycle-environment "Development" \
                                   --organization "MyOrg"
Notes & checks
  • Ensure the specified lifecycle environment exists.
  • Verify task history for success and check the Content View versions in target environment.
  • Remember: versions are immutable snapshots; promotion copies, not edits.
Pro tip
Script the list-and-promote sequence with validation to avoid accidental promotions to Production.

screens.title: Registering a Host with subscription-manager
screens.narratorSegment: Registering a RHEL host to Satellite is how you bring a system under central control. The client must have the subscription-manager package installed; that provides the command line tools to register, attach entitlements, and list available repositories. On many RHEL systems you install it with the package manager and then run subscription-manager register. A practical and recommended pattern is to generate an activation key in Satellite configured with organization, Content View, Lifecycle Environment, and subscriptions, then run subscription-manager register with that activation key. This single command enrolls the host with all those settings applied, reducing manual steps. Example: run 'sudo dnf install subscription-manager -y' then 'sudo subscription-manager register --org="MyOrg" --activationkey="rhel8_dev_key" --serverurl="https://satellite. example. com" --baseurl="https://satellite. example. com/pulp/content" --force'. A common misconception is that registration automatically attaches all subscriptions; you must ensure the activation key includes the required subscriptions or attach them after registration. After registering, verify with 'subscription-manager status' and 'dnf repolist' that repos point to your Satellite Content View. What verification steps will you include in your standard operating procedure? In practical terms, install subscription-manager, register with an activation key, and verify repos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Registration
keyIdea.text: Use subscription-manager and activation keys to enroll a host with the correct organization, Content View, and environment.

content.html:
Process Flow › Register host
Install and register
sudo dnf install subscription-manager -y

# Replace values with your Satellite FQDN and activation key
sudo subscription-manager clean
sudo subscription-manager register --org="MyOrg" --activationkey="rhel8_dev_key" --serverurl="https://satellite.example.com" --baseurl="https://satellite.example.com/pulp/content" --force

# Verify
sudo subscription-manager status
sudo dnf repolist
Checks & pitfalls
  • Ensure activation key includes the correct Content View and subscriptions.
  • Run 'dnf repolist' to confirm repos are Satellite-provided.
  • If a host is not subscribed, it will not receive updates — verify entitlements in Satellite.
Analogy
Activation keys are like a registration template: they apply a set of attributes in one command.

screens.title: Activation Keys and Their Role
screens.narratorSegment: Activation keys are powerful tools that encapsulate registration parameters and subscriptions so hosts enroll with consistent settings. When you create an activation key in Satellite you can pre-select the organization, location, Content View, Lifecycle Environment, and subscriptions to attach. This removes manual mistakes and speeds large-scale enrollment. A concrete example: create an activation key named 'rhel8_dev_key' that selects 'Base RHEL 8 & Custom Apps' as the Content View and 'Development' as the lifecycle environment, then add the required RHEL 8 subscription. Using that key, an admin runs subscription-manager register with the key and the host appears in Satellite already assigned to the correct Content View and environment. A common misconception is treating activation keys as permanent credentials — you should rotate keys and scope their permissions. Also, ensure activation keys include subscriptions to avoid 'Partially Subscribed' hosts. Final takeaway: activation keys encode policy at enrollment time, so design keys carefully to match the lifecycle stage and compliance needs. keyIdea.text: A reusable registration object that applies organization, Content View, environment, and subscriptions during host registration.

content.html:
Definition › Activation Key
What it is
A pre-configured registration artifact that applies organization, Content View, environment and subscriptions when used during subscription-manager register.
  • Scopes the host to the correct lifecycle environment at registration.
  • Adds required subscriptions automatically if configured.
  • Reduces manual configuration and enrollment errors.
Security & governance
Treat activation keys like scoped credentials: rotate them, limit their permissions, and attach only the necessary subscriptions. Avoid over-privileged keys for broad registration tasks.
Key Takeaway
Use activation keys to automate and standardize registrations so hosts are placed in the right environment from day one.

screens.title: Subscription Status and Candlepin Entitlements
screens.narratorSegment: Subscription status indicates whether a host has the proper entitlements to access repositories. Satellite communicates with Candlepin to track entitlements. Hosts show statuses such as Subscribed, Partially Subscribed, or Expired. If a host is Partially Subscribed it may lack some slotted entitlements and therefore cannot access all repos it needs, which prevents package updates from applying. An example: a host registered without the correct pool attached will show Partially Subscribed and dnf repolist may be missing Satellite repos. A misconception is assuming registration always equals full subscription; it does not. Activation keys can include subscriptions, but you must verify availability in your manifest and that pools are not exhausted. From an operational perspective, regularly audit host subscription status in Satellite and reconcile any 'Partially Subscribed' hosts by attaching the missing entitlements. The practical question to carry forward is: how will you monitor subscription pools to ensure new hosts can be fully subscribed at enrollment? In practical terms, why 'subscribed' vs 'partially subscribed' matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subscription status
keyIdea.text: Subscription state determines repository access; audit and attach required entitlements to avoid partial subscriptions.

content.html:
Comparison › Subscribed vs Partially Subscribed
Subscribed
Host has required entitlements and can access all repos included in its Content View and lifecycle environment.
  • Allows dnf to see Satellite-hosted repos.
  • Receives applicable errata and package updates.
  • Typically shows 'Subscribed' in Satellite host details.
Partially Subscribed / Expired
Host is missing some entitlements or subscriptions have expired, which blocks repository access and updates.
  • Often due to exhausted pools or missing subscription attachment.
  • Fix by attaching the correct pool or updating the subscription manifest.
  • Verify with 'subscription-manager status' and Satellite host details.
Operational tip
Automate subscription audits and alert on 'Partially Subscribed' hosts so you can remediate before updates are required.

screens.title: Applying Errata and Package Updates
screens.narratorSegment: Applying errata and package updates is the action that completes the lifecycle: once a Content View version containing new errata is promoted to an environment, hosts in that environment should receive the updates. Satellite centralizes errata visibility under Content → Errata or Hosts → Content Hosts. You can select errata and push updates via remote execution, or let clients pull updates. On the client, common commands are 'sudo dnf updateinfo list security' and 'sudo dnf update' to apply patches. A concrete example: after promoting a new Content View version to Development, check 'updateinfo list' to see security, bugfix, or enhancement errata, run tests, and then apply updates. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: A few recurring mistakes cause most production surprises. First, failing to publish a new Content View version after syncing repositories means hosts remain on the prior immutable version and do not receive updated errata. Second, using activation keys without the necessary subscriptions or with an incorrect Content View assigns hosts incorrectly, causing missing repositories. Third, misordering environment parents or promoting a version directly to Production without passing through Development or QA bypasses testing. To prevent these, adopt verification steps: after publish, confirm the new version appears in the Content View versions list, then promote to Development and run your test suite. When registering hosts, perform 'subscription-manager status' and 'dnf repolist' to confirm repo endpoints. Also regularly audit subscription pools and manifest capacity to avoid exhausted entitlements. In larger deployments, automate promotions and use CI checks to gate promotions. Final reflective question: what automated checks could you implement to block accidental direct promotion to Production? screens.title: How the Pieces Fit: Satellite, Capsule, and Hosts
screens.narratorSegment: Operationally, Satellite coordinates content synchronization, Content Views, lifecycle environments, and host management. In many deployments Capsules act as regional content mirrors and proxied registration endpoints, reducing cross-site bandwidth and latency. Hosts register to either the Satellite server or a Capsule, inherit their Content View and lifecycle environment via activation key or manual assignment, and then retrieve packages from the Capsule or Satellite. A concrete scenario: an organization with multiple datacenters uses Capsules in each datacenter. You publish and promote a Content View on Satellite; the Capsule syncs the promoted content and serves hosts locally. A misconception is assuming hosts always pull from Satellite directly — well-configured deployments prefer Capsules to scale. From a governance standpoint, ensure activation keys point to the intended Capsule or server and that Content Views are consistent across sites. Consider how you would validate that a Capsule has synchronized the promoted Content View and that hosts in that site receive the updated packages. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we build a reliable content delivery pipeline using Lifecycle Environments and host management in Red Hat Satellite. You will learn what a lifecycle environment is, how to create an environment path that models Development, QA, and Production, and why promoting versioned Content Views through those stages reduces risk. We will cover host registration using activation keys so that a client is automatically assigned an organization, a Content View, and the correct environment. You will also see how subscription status and Candlepin entitlements control whether a host can receive updates. Finally, we'll walk through applying errata and package updates from Satellite to managed hosts. For example, a security patch synchronized to Satellite must be published in a new Content View version and promoted through lower stages before Production sees it. That practice ensures changes are tested and predictable. As you proceed, keep an eye out for two common mistakes: forgetting to publish new Content View versions after synchronization, and misconfigured activation keys that assign hosts to the wrong environment. By the end you'll understand the lifecycle flow, practical host registration, and how to keep systems compliant and patched without disrupting production.

These four learning objectives map directly to practical tasks you'll perform in Satellite. First, you will define and configure Lifecycle Environments so they represent stages like Development, QA, and Production. That means creating environment paths and setting parents so promotions flow predictably. Second, you will associate Content Views with lifecycle environments and practice publishing and promoting Content View versions so hosts receive only approved content. Third, you will register RHEL hosts using subscription-manager and activation keys, ensuring hosts are assigned to the correct Content View and environment at enrollment. Fourth, you will manage host subscriptions and apply errata and package updates through Satellite, verifying entitlement status and using remote execution where appropriate. Each objective is paired with a short mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember the workflow. For example, think of promotion as a conveyor belt where versions move only when tested. Throughout, we emphasize why testing in lower environments prevents outages and how activation keys reduce human error during registration. By the end you will be able to demonstrate these tasks in a terminal-first lab and explain the consequences of common mistakes.

In addition to conceptual goals, this screen frames each objective as a practical task you will perform. Defining lifecycle environments means creating the path a Content View will follow, and you'll do this in the Satellite UI so promotion order is explicit. Associating Content Views is an operational skill: you'll publish a version, then promote it from Library to Development and onward, watching that hosts only receive updates when you move the version. Registering hosts is hands-on: install subscription-manager, use an activation key, and verify the client's repolist points to Satellite. Managing subscriptions involves auditing entitlements and attaching or detaching subscriptions so hosts show as Subscribed and can access repos. Applying errata and updates completes the loop: after promotion, trigger updates and confirm hosts receive the package versions from the correct environment. For each objective you'll also learn one common pitfall and a verification step so you can prove competency in an audit or lab demo. These skills together form the operational workflow for safe, repeatable content delivery.

A Lifecycle Environment is an explicit stage that represents where a Content View version is allowed to be used. Think of it as a labeled container — Development, QA, Staging, Production — that controls the repositories and package snapshots visible to enrolled hosts. Defining environments establishes a promotion path: you decide that content moves from Library to Development, then QA, and finally Production, and Satellite enforces that flow. A concrete example: after synchronizing security errata into Satellite, you publish a new Content View version. That version initially exists in the Library. You must publish it and then promote it to Development so testers can validate the updates. Only after validation do you promote it onward. A common misconception is believing synchronization alone makes updates available to production. It does not. Content View versions are immutable snapshots; only publishing a new version and promoting it makes the new content visible to a target environment. Why this matters in practice: it prevents accidental rollout of untested packages to production. As a closing checkpoint, ask yourself: what would happen if you promoted directly to Production without a Development stage?

Creating a lifecycle environment path is a simple but crucial process. In Satellite you go to Content → Lifecycle Environments and add named environments. Each environment you add can specify a parent, which creates the promotion path. A typical setup is Library as the root, Development with parent Library, and Production with parent Development. The practical effect is that when you promote a Content View version you choose a target environment and Satellite enforces where that copy appears. Concrete example: create Development with parent Library, then create Production with parent Development. Now publish CV version 2.0. Promote 2.0 to Development and test. Only after testing do you promote 2.0 to Production. A common error is reversing parent relationships or creating isolated environments that break the flow. Another pitfall is treating Library as a deployable environment — it is a repository of synchronized content, not an environment for production hosts. Verify your path by reviewing the environment tree and confirming that promotion actions show the expected next step. How would you validate that a new environment path allows promotion from Dev to Prod without bypassing QA?

The hammer CLI provides a reproducible way to list Content View versions and promote a specific version into a lifecycle environment. The first useful command is listing versions for a given Content View so you can identify the version string to promote. Next, use the promote command, specifying the target lifecycle environment and organization. A concrete example from the chapter shows promoting version 1.0 of a Content View called 'Base RHEL 8 & Custom Apps' to Development. Running these commands in automation ensures repeatability and records the action in Satellite's task history. A common misconception is thinking promotion mutates a version — promotions copy immutable versions into the target environment rather than modifying the original. If you automate promotions, include checks that the target environment exists and that the version was published. As a closing thought, decide whether CLI promotion or UI promotion fits your workflow better: CLI is scriptable and auditable, UI is visual and helpful for ad-hoc checks. Which method would you choose for a large-scale automated pipeline? Registering a RHEL host to Satellite is how you bring a system under central control. These are the essential concepts you should remember. First, a Lifecycle Environment is a named stage that gates which Content View versions a host may use, enabling a controlled promotion path from Library through lower environments to Production. Second, Content View Promotion is the act of publishing an immutable version and copying it into a target lifecycle environment so hosts assigned to that environment can access its repositories. Third, Host Registration links a host to Satellite, assigns organization, location, Content View, and lifecycle environment, and is often automated with activation keys. Keep these concepts clear: promotion controls visibility, versions are immutable, and activation keys encode enrollment policy. Use these anchors when planning changes so you avoid the common mistakes of skipping publish, misconfiguring activation keys, or running out of subscriptions. Use this quick reference when working in Satellite. Third, Errata Application: the controlled deployment of security, bugfix, or enhancement updates; remember to publish and promote Content View versions so errata reach intended hosts.
